strengths: Proposes an information-geometric formulation of SBDD by modeling molecules as composite exponential-family distributions and using e-geodesics under the Fisher-Rao metric to unify continuous coordinates and discrete atom/bond types.

Identifies the practical singularity of static Dirac endpoints and proposes a dynamic endpoint schedule; ablation shows the naive fixed-Dirac exponential geodesic fails badly, supporting the motivation for an evolving target.

Reports strong PoseBusters validity (93.4%), very low strain energy, and improved scaffold-level metrics on MolGenBench, with detailed PoseBusters breakdowns and bond/angle/torsion distribution comparisons.

Includes ablation studies on the evolving endpoint, Dirichlet parameterization, smoothing coefficients, and explicit bond generation, plus training/sampling algorithms and implementation hyperparameters.
Provides a reasonably honest limitations discussion regarding low absolute MolGenBench hit rates and poor generalization to unseen targets.
weaknesses: Core theoretical claims are not adequately supported: Eq. (9) for the induced sample-space velocity field is not rigorously derived, the 'Fisher flow matching equivalence' proof in Appendix F.3 does not match the implemented loss, and the SLDM connection is superficial. The e-geodesic itself is essentially linear interpolation in natural parameters, which is already central to BFN/PIF-style methods, so novelty is incremental.

Serious mathematical inconsistency in the Dirichlet path: at t=1 the schedule gives alpha = v_M (one-hot with zero entries for non-target classes), which is not a valid Dirichlet distribution. Sampling from this endpoint is undefined; no epsilon or fallback is specified, undermining the claim of a valid probability path.

Training and sampling algorithms contain critical errors and inconsistencies: Algorithm 1 line 15 writes ||x_M - x_M||^2 instead of involving the prediction; the network outputs clean coordinates/types/bonds while the main text says it predicts terminal parameters; the step mapping predicted clean types to \hat{alpha}_t is missing; and Eq. (11) appears to use reverse KL or has a sign error relative to the stated forward KL.

Evaluation fairness and attribution are weak: baselines are taken from released samples rather than retrained under the same architecture/protocol; EvoEGF-Mol uses a Unitransformer-with-edge base model from MolPilot and different sampling steps; no comparison is made to recent SOTA such as PIF, MolPilot, FLOWR, DynamicFlow, or ECloudGen. Gains may be due to architecture or sampling rather than the proposed flow.

The strain-energy results are anomalous and unexplained: EvoEGF-Mol reports 8.94/25.96/56.65 versus CrossDock reference 34/107/196. Generated molecules being far less strained than reference crystal ligands is suspicious and may indicate metric artifact, relaxed non-bioactive conformations, or an unfair comparison. This directly challenges the 'remarkable geometric precision' claim.

Binding-affinity results do not support the strongest claims: EvoEGF-Mol is worse than MolCRAFT on Vina Score (-6.14 vs -6.55) and Vina Min (-6.98 vs -7.21), only marginally better on Vina Dock. The abstract's 'interaction fidelity' and 'significantly outperforms' language is overstated for an SBDD method whose primary goal is binding.

MolGenBench improvements are very small in absolute terms (e.g., Hit Fraction around 0.01% and Hit Recovery 7 vs 3 molecules for MolCRAFT in the appendix), so the 'real-world applicability' contribution is limited despite the scaffold-level gains.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code or data/evaluation scripts are provided; key details are missing or contradictory (network output parameterization, sampling protocol, how baselines were sampled, whether filtering is identical). The algorithms as written would not reproduce the method.

Presentation quality is poor in places: many typos and equation errors, inconsistent notation (x_M vs x^* vs \hat{x}_M; \eta vs \theta), confusing Table 2 headers, text/table mismatches (e.g., '72 and 33 targets'), duplicated/incorrect references with wrong years, and vague figure captions. These make the paper hard to verify.

The conceptual claim that a product of independent exponential-family components captures structural-chemical synergy is not demonstrated. The distribution remains factorized given parameters; any coupling comes from the neural network, not the information-geometric construction. This weakens the central motivation.

strengths: The information-geometric framing is well-motivated and gives a coherent, intuitive picture: molecules as composite exponential-family distributions, generative paths as e-geodesics under the Fisher–Rao metric, and the 'Dynamic Endpoint' as a way to keep the path in the interior of the manifold. The narrative is easy to follow and connects SBDD to a principled geometric view.

Several CrossDock results are genuinely strong: PB-Valid 93.4% (close to the 95.0% re-docked reference), best Vina Dock (-7.72), best connectivity (97.1%), and dramatically lower strain energy (quartiles 8.94/25.96/56.65 vs. 83/195/510 for MolCRAFT). The PoseBusters breakdown (Table 5) and the geometry-distribution plots (Figs. 9–11) substantiate improved local geometric fidelity.

The paper includes an ablation study and a second, real-world-oriented benchmark (MolGenBench), and it reports an honest limitations discussion acknowledging that absolute scaffold/hit rates remain near zero and that generalization to unseen targets is weak.
The observation that SLDM can be recovered as a regularized (constant-variance, linear-mean) special case of EGF is a neat, if minor, conceptual link.
weaknesses: The central novelty is overstated. The paper itself states the method is implemented within the BFN/PIF progressive-parameter-refinement framework; the only substantive change is the schedule sigma_1(t)=lambda(1-t) and alpha_1(t)=(1-lambda(1-t))e_k + lambda(1-t)/K. Linear interpolation in natural parameters under the e-connection is a known property of exponential families, and the 'evolving target' is essentially a standard variance/concentration schedule that every diffusion/flow model already possesses. The information-geometric apparatus therefore reads largely as reinterpretation of an existing training scheme rather than a new generative mechanism.

The theoretical claims are not rigorously supported. Appendix F.2's derivation of the sample-space velocity field is hand-wavy ('Generalizing this to exponential families...', 'we require...', 'Crucially, the presence of the term...') and never actually solves the continuity equation for a general exponential family; the Moore-Penrose form in Eq. 9 is asserted. Appendix F.3's claim that the loss 'is equivalent to Fisher Flow Matching' rests on an unproven local Taylor expansion of KL and an informal identification of terms. The SLDM reduction (App. D) is essentially trivial (setting sigma_0=sigma_1=eps forces a constant-variance, linear-mean path).

There is an internal inconsistency in the loss definition that matters for reproducibility: Eq. 10 defines the coordinate loss with ||x* - x_hat||^2, whereas Appendix G and Algorithm 1 use ||mu_1 - mu_hat_1||^2, and Eq. 10 simultaneously says the network learns a denoiser mu_hat_1. Algorithm 1 line 15 even writes ||x_M - x_M||^2 (trivially zero), indicating a copy error. These make the exact objective ambiguous.

The pivotal ablation is confounded. The 'naive EGF' baseline (sigma_1=0.05) collapses to PB-Valid 64.1% and a positive (repulsive) Vina score of +1.67. A well-tuned fixed-variance schedule should not produce repulsive molecules; this strongly suggests the baseline was under-tuned or mis-implemented, so the ablation does not cleanly establish that the 'evolving' strategy is the cause of the gains (the appendix's own loss curves show the regime is 'ill-conditioned' either way).

Recent and relevant SBDD baselines (FLOWR, DynamicFlow, ECloudGen, MolPilot) are discussed in Related Work but never compared. The only strong contemporary baseline is MolCRAFT, and EvoEGF-Mol is actually worse on Vina Score (-6.14 vs -6.55) and Vina Min (-6.98 vs -7.21); the headline affinity claims ('improved binding poses') therefore rest on a single metric (Vina Dock) with a small margin.

On MolGenBench the absolute performance is near-zero (Hit Rates <5%, Hit Fraction ~1%, zero recovery on unseen targets), so the 'real-world utility' claims are marginal in absolute terms even if relatively better. The practical significance is thus weaker than the framing implies.

Presentation and reproducibility problems: numerous reference errors (duplicate/mismatched years, e.g., Cremer 2024/2025, Cheng 2024 listed twice, Bemis & Murcko 2024 vs 1996, Eberhardt 2024 vs 2021), an introduction reference to a nonexistent 'Sec.B' (Sec. 3.1.1 is mislabeled 3.1.2 in the text), typos ('a efficient strategy'), and low-quality/illegible figures. No code, model, or data release is mentioned, and the exact schedules, loss weighting, and conditioning details are insufficient to reliably reproduce.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel information-geometric perspective for SBDD, modeling a molecule as a composite exponential-family distribution whose components evolve jointly along exponential geodesics under the Fisher-Rao metric. The closure result for product exponential families (Theorem 1, Appendix F.1) gives a principled way to couple continuous coordinates and discrete categories within a single statistical manifold, which is a fresh framing relative to decoupled Euclidean/categorical diffusion.

The identification of the Dirac-endpoint singularity is well motivated and clearly illustrated (Fig. 2, Appendix B). The proposed dynamic endpoint (Eq. 7) is a simple, interpretable, and effective fix that keeps the path in the manifold interior, and the paper honestly connects this to prior work by showing SLDM is a zero-curvature special case (Appendix D).

Empirical results are strong and consistent. On CrossDock, EvoEGF-Mol attains PB-Valid 93.4% (vs 84.6% for the best baseline), by far the best strain-energy quartiles (8.94/25.96/56.65 vs 83/195/510 for MolCRAFT), the best Vina Dock (-7.72), and the best connectivity (97.1%). Bond-length/angle/torsion and substructure distributions (Tables 6-8, Figs. 9-11) closely match references, and the PoseBusters breakdown (Table 5) is comprehensive.

The ablation (Table 4) is decisive: the naive static-Dirac EGF collapses (64.1% PB-Valid, positive Vina +1.67), while the evolving endpoint recovers 93.4% PB-Valid and -6.14 Vina under the same backbone, isolating the effect of the proposed mechanism. The Dirichlet parameterization, smoothing coefficient, and explicit bond-generation ablations are also informative.

The real-world MolGenBench evaluation (Table 2) shows consistent improvement on scaffold-level metrics (Pass Rate 31.79/29.61%, Hit Recovery 72/33), and the limitations section honestly reports the very low absolute hit fractions and the failure to generalize to unseen targets, which is a responsible treatment of negative results.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported by explicit schedules, optimizer settings, feature encodings, and training/inference pseudocode (Algorithms 1-2), and loss derivations are given in Appendix G.
weaknesses: The practical mechanism largely reduces to a time-varying target schedule within the BFN/PIF progressive-parameter-refinement framework the authors themselves cite. Since Eq. 7 is still linear interpolation in natural parameters, the delta over BFN is essentially the time-varying endpoint; the paper would benefit from stating more explicitly what is inherited versus new, and from an ablation that isolates the 'geometric coupling' claim (the alleged alleviation of temporal mismatch between geometry and chemistry is not directly tested).

The headline comparison against published baselines is confounded by architecture: EvoEGF-Mol uses a recent unitransformer-with-edge backbone (MolPilot), while baselines use heterogeneous backbones. The in-house ablation mitigates this, but the claim that EvoEGF-Mol 'significantly outperforms traditional SBDD generative models' is not fully clean, and binding affinity (Vina Score/Min) is actually second to MolCRAFT, so superiority claims need qualification.

Several derivations are informal. The induced velocity field (Eq. 9 / Appendix F.2) introduces a scaling matrix C_t that is asserted to be 'determined by' the parameter velocity but is never determined, and the construction via pseudoinverse is not rigorously justified. The SLDM 'horocycle/zero-curvature' argument (Appendix D.2) and the singularity claims in Appendix B are stated more than proven.

Notation is inconsistent and contains clear typos that hurt readability: Eq. 10 uses x* while Algorithm 1 line 15 writes ||x_M - x_M||^2 (should be the predicted target); Sec. 3.3 conflates alpha_t with alpha_1(t) in the Dirichlet schedule; the text in Sec. 3.1.2 refers to 'Sec. B' for the singularity discussion that actually lives in Appendix B.

No code or model release is mentioned, and given the complexity of the schedules and backbone, independent reproduction would be non-trivial; the comparison relies on released baseline samples rather than re-run baselines.

Theoretically important claims (e.g., that e-geodesic coupling of atom identity and geometry yields a 'geometrically consistent' joint refinement, and that intermediate distributions remain well-conditioned) are argued qualitatively and illustrated on 1-D toy Gaussians rather than demonstrated on the actual molecular manifolds.

strengths: Introduces a principled information-geometric formulation for SBDD, representing molecules as product exponential-family distributions (Gaussian for coordinates, Dirichlet for atom/bond types) and using e-geodesics in a unified natural-parameter space to synchronize continuous and discrete generation.

Identifies and addresses a real problem: static Dirac targets cause singularity and premature collapse. The dynamic-endpoint strategy is supported by an ablation where a fixed-endpoint EGF variant drops to 64.1% PB-Valid versus 93.4% for the proposed evolving endpoint.

Achieves strong geometric validity on CrossDock: 93.4% PB-Valid, near-perfect PoseBusters checks for sanitization, bond lengths/angles, and aromaticity, and substantially lower strain-energy quartiles (8.94/25.96/56.65) than all baselines.
Shows consistent improvements on MolGenBench scaffold metrics over the chosen baselines: Pass Rate 31.79% vs 23.07% (MolCRAFT), Hit Recovery 72 vs 66, and Hit Fraction 1.08% vs 0.70%.
Includes useful ablations on the evolving strategy, Dirichlet parameterization, smoothing coefficient, explicit bond modeling, and sampling steps, which support several design choices.
Provides a theoretical connection showing SLDM is a special case of the proposed EGF under regularized static endpoints, and gives a Fisher-Rao local interpretation of the KL objective.
Discusses limitations and ethics: notes low absolute hit rates in MolGenBench, potential misuse for toxic compounds, and the need for wet-lab validation.
weaknesses: Omits the most relevant SOTA baseline, MolPilot. The authors explicitly admit in Appendix F that EvoEGF-Mol obtains a lower PB-Valid score than MolPilot, yet MolPilot is not included in the main tables. Other recent SBDD flow-matching methods (FLOWR, DynamicFlow, ECloudGen) are also absent, undermining claims of superiority and 'reference-level' performance.

The central claim that a unified natural-parameter space and synchronized refinement drive the gains is not directly ablated. There is no controlled comparison against separately scheduled Gaussian and Dirichlet flows with the same architecture; the observed improvements could largely stem from the dynamic endpoint alone.

The dynamic endpoint schedules (\hat{\sigma}_1(t)=\lambda(1-t), \hat{\alpha}_1(t)=(1-\lambda(1-t))e_k + \lambda(1-t)/K) are heuristic and tuned. No principled derivation from information geometry is given, and the claim of automatic Fisher-calibrated supervision is overstated because \lambda still balances modalities and must be tuned.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds are reported. With only 100 test targets and single-run evaluations, the statistical significance of the reported metric differences is unknown.

Mathematical and notational inconsistencies hinder reproducibility: Eq. 12 uses \hat{\sigma}_1(t)^4 while Appendix I uses \sigma_1^4; notation switches between \ddot{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_1 and \hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_1; Eq. 8 contains \dot{\dot{\boldsymbol{\eta}}}_1; and the construction of \hat{\alpha}_t from the network output \hat{v}_M is not specified. The abstract's code link is missing.

Overclaims in the abstract and introduction ('significantly outperforms traditional SBDD generative models across multiple benchmarks') are not supported for binding affinity: Vina Score, Vina Min, and Vina Dock are worse than MolCRAFT, and PB-Valid is lower than the cited MolPilot.

The method is incremental, combining existing ideas from e-geodesic flow matching, Bayesian Flow Networks / Parameter Interpolation Flow, and dynamic endpoint regularization. Novelty is moderate and primarily in the application-specific scheduling rather than in a fundamentally new framework.

Practical significance on MolGenBench remains limited: absolute Hit Rates are below 5% and Hit Fractions around 1%, which the authors acknowledge but which underscores a large gap to real-world drug discovery.

strengths: Novel and principled information-geometric framing: modeling a molecule as a product of exponential-family distributions (Gaussian for coordinates, Dirichlet for atom/bond types) and evolving them along e-geodesics in a shared natural-parameter space is an interesting and coherent way to synchronize heterogeneous modalities.

The paper clearly identifies a real problem (the Dirac-target singularity causing premature trajectory collapse, Appendix B) and proposes a well-motivated remedy (dynamic, gradually concentrating endpoints). Appendix D's argument that dynamic endpoints are not reducible to nonlinear time reparameterizations is a useful clarification.

Geometric/physical validity results are genuinely strong: PB-Valid of 93.4% approaches the 95.0% reference, median strain energy of 25.96 is far below MolCRAFT (195) and TargetDiff (1243), and the PoseBusters breakdown (Table 5) shows near-perfect chemical and local-geometry validity.

The limitations discussion is honest: the authors explicitly acknowledge that absolute MolGenBench performance is low (Scaffold Hit Rates <5%) and that geometric plausibility alone does not bridge the drug-discovery efficiency gap.

Evaluation protocol is comparatively fair: baselines are scored from released samples (Qiu et al. 2025; Cao et al. 2025) under a shared metric pipeline, and ablations isolate the evolving-endpoint, Dirichlet-parameterization, smoothing, and bond-diffusion choices.
weaknesses: The most relevant SOTA baseline, MolPilot (Qiu et al., 2025), is omitted from the main comparison tables, even though the authors use its released samples to evaluate the other baselines and explicitly concede in Appendix F that 'EvoEGF-Mol obtains a slightly lower PB-Valid score than MolPilot.' Excluding the direct competitor that beats the method on the headline metric while including weaker baselines is selective reporting that undermines the central empirical claim.

The headline claim that EvoEGF-Mol 'significantly outperforms traditional SBDD generative models' is overstated. In Table 1, EvoEGF-Mol's Vina Score (-6.14) is worse than MolCRAFT (-6.55), and its Vina Dock improvement is marginal; gains are concentrated in validity and strain energy rather than binding affinity.

Novelty is incremental. The training/inference machinery is explicitly 'inspired by' and 'compatible with' BFN and PIF, and the main new element (the evolving endpoint) is essentially a target-schedule/regularization design choice; the paper itself notes SLDM and PIF as close relatives.

The claim that SLDM is a special case of EGF is only sketched via a one-dimensional Gaussian example in Appendix E, with no general proof; similarly the connection between the Fisher-Rao flow and the actual training objective is loose (the network directly regresses endpoints, and the 'Fisher-calibrated' benefit is only a local second-order KL interpretation in Appendix H.3).

Presentation is weak and would impede reuse: notation for the evolving endpoint is inconsistent (eta-double-dot, eta-hat, eta-tilde used interchangeably), Eq. 8 contains a spurious double-dot on the endpoint velocity, Eq. 12 uses sigma-hat^4 while the derivation (Eq. 45) uses sigma^4, and Algorithm 2 is garbled with placeholder symbols that do not parse.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract states 'Code is available at' but no link is given, and key details (e.g., the exact endpoint network heads, how hat-eta_1 maps to a valid next-step distribution during sampling) are underspecified.

MolGenBench results are only compelling at the relative level; the absolute numbers are near-zero (Table 3 Hit Fraction ~0.01%, Not-target Hit Recovery = 0), and the authors' own text concedes these are far from practical utility, so the 'real-world applicability' framing is not strongly supported by the evidence.

The theoretical singularity argument and the practical schedule are somewhat decoupled: the paper never demonstrates that the proposed lambda(1-t) schedule is optimal or principled relative to alternatives beyond a small ablation (lambda in {0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4}), and the choice is presented as empirically tuned rather than derived from the geometry.

strengths: Introduces a novel information-geometric formulation for SBDD: molecules are represented as product exponential-family distributions (Gaussian for coordinates, Dirichlet for atom/bond types), and generation follows e-geodesics in a unified natural-parameter space. This provides a principled way to synchronize continuous and discrete modalities, addressing the mismatch of separately designed probability paths.

Proposes a dynamic endpoint strategy to avoid the singularity of Dirac targets on statistical manifolds. The ablation is striking: naive EGF with a fixed Dirac target (σ1=0.05) collapses to 64.1% PB-Valid and even yields a positive Vina score (+1.67), while the evolving endpoint achieves 93.4% PB-Valid, validating the core design choice.

Achieves strong geometric and physical validity results on CrossDock: 93.4% PB-Valid (close to the 95.0% reference), 98.6% connected, and dramatically lower strain energy (median 25.96 vs. 195 for MolCRAFT and 1243 for TargetDiff). This indicates more physically plausible molecular conformations, which is valuable for SBDD.

Provides a thorough empirical study: CrossDock and MolGenBench evaluations, multiple metrics (PoseBusters, Vina, strain energy, scaffold recovery), ablations on the evolving strategy, Dirichlet parameterization, smoothing coefficients, bond diffusion, and sampling steps. The intermediate-state analysis further shows faster emergence of valid molecular prototypes.

Honest discussion of limitations: the paper explicitly acknowledges that absolute MolGenBench hit rates remain very low (e.g., scaffold hit rates <5%, molecule hit fraction 0.01%) and that geometric plausibility alone cannot bridge the gap to practical drug discovery. This transparency is commendable.

Includes useful theoretical derivations: the Gaussian and Dirichlet loss functions from KL divergence, the local Fisher-Rao interpretation of the one-step KL objective, and a demonstration that dynamic endpoints are not equivalent to non-linear time reparameterization.
weaknesses: Missing comparison to the most relevant SOTA baselines. MolPilot (Qiu et al., 2025) is a direct SBDD competitor with modality-specific optimal scheduling, and the paper admits in Appendix F that EvoEGF-Mol obtains a slightly lower PB-Valid score than MolPilot. Yet MolPilot is not included in the main tables. Similarly, PIF (Jin et al., 2025) directly inspired the training framework, but no empirical comparison is provided. This weakens the claim of superiority and makes the contribution harder to assess.

Baseline fairness is questionable: baselines are evaluated from released samples from Qiu et al. (2025) rather than retrained under identical settings (same architecture, sampling steps, and data splits). The paper reports no variance across runs or statistical significance tests, so the reported improvements may be confounded by different sampling budgets or hyperparameters.

The claim that the KL objective automatically calibrates relative supervision strengths across modalities ('Fisher-calibrated') is not empirically validated against alternative weighting schemes. The ablation varies only the Dirichlet parameterization, not manual loss weights. The local Fisher-Rao expansion is second-order; the exact training loss may not yield the claimed automatic calibration in practice.

The theoretical connection to SLDM in Appendix E appears oversimplified. The claim that SLDM corresponds to a constant variance σt=ε may not match SLDM's actual forward process, where variance typically varies with t. This undermines the geometric interpretation of SLDM as a horocycle or flat submanifold.

Presentation and notation issues hinder readability and reproducibility: Eq. 7 and 8 use \ddot{\eta}_1(t) inconsistently with \tilde{\eta}_1(t) and \hat{\eta}_1(t) elsewhere; Eq. 8 contains a likely typo \dot{\dot{\eta}}_1(t). Algorithm 2 is garbled with duplicated variable names and missing superscripts, making the sampling procedure difficult to follow. The abstract says 'Code is available at' but no URL is provided.

Reproducibility is not fully supported: no random seeds, no hyperparameter search details, no computational cost beyond training time, and no code link. The mapping from the network's predicted clean labels to the Dirichlet parameters \hat{\alpha}_t is not explicitly defined in the main text, requiring readers to infer from BFN/PIF.

The dynamic endpoint schedule is heuristic: \hat{\sigma}_1(t)=\lambda(1-t) and \hat{\alpha}_1(t)=(1-\lambda(1-t))e_k + \lambda(1-t)/K. The linear decay is not theoretically justified, and other schedules may be better. The smoothing coefficient \lambda=0.2 is tuned but no sensitivity analysis across datasets or targets is provided.

The practical significance of the MolGenBench results is limited by very low absolute hit rates. Although the method outperforms listed baselines, the absolute scaffold hit fraction is around 1% and molecule hit fraction is 0.01%. The main text still emphasizes 'superior performance' without fully contextualizing that current performance is far from real-world utility.
